extracted.intended_audience: readers of Popular Science Monthly; general public interested in anthropology, medicine, and social criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing cultural practices of bodily modification (teeth, skull, feet, corseting, etc.) with attention to purpose, method, permanence, health effects, and aesthetic/social meaning. The piece surveys examples worldwide and weighs functional/medical consequences against fashion and social pressures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose / Intent (fashion vs ritual)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguishes whether a bodily alteration is done for ornament/fashion, as part of rites of initiation, or as a propitiatory sacrifice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given: tooth modifications as fashion/ornament; knocking out front teeth in Australia sometimes part of initiation rites; finger amputation often part of initiatory ceremony or expiation. Use intent to categorize practice and to judge social meaning rather than purely aesthetic value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of invasiveness and permanence
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the modification affects comparatively external/flexible parts (hair, ears, nose, lips, superficial tooth filing) or induces permanent structural alterations of bony framework and internal organs (cranial deformation, foot-binding, tight-lacing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay contrasts trivial external modifications with those causing permanent skeletal change; invasiveness implies greater potential for health consequences and long-term social consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Age at application and timing
rubrics_metrics.description: When the alteration is begun (e.g., immediately after birth, childhood around five years, infancy) and how long the process is continued (e.g., cranial bandaging for 8–12 months).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early-life procedures (infancy/childhood) are noted to produce more permanent changes; timing is central to whether the body can be molded or will recover its natural form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method / technical classification
rubrics_metrics.description: The specific technique used to alter form (e.g., chipping/fileing teeth; staining; drilling and inserting metal plugs; flattening skull between boards; circular constricting bandages; binding feet; tight-lacing corsets; bearing-reins on horses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article gives detailed descriptions and figures (e.g., two principal divisions of cranial deformity: flattening between boards vs constricting bandages). Method informs expected morphological outcome and risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resulting morphological pattern / symmetry
rubrics_metrics.description: The characteristic shape produced (flattened occiput with lateral bulging/obliquity; circular constriction producing elongation without lateral bulging; serrated/pointed teeth; hoof-like bound feet; narrowed waist and altered thoracic cavity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize compensatory changes (flattening causes lateral bulging) and whether deformation preserves bilateral symmetry or produces obliquity; useful for classification and assessing degree of alteration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional impact on important organs and motion
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the alteration impairs or alters the function of organs or locomotion (e.g., brain accommodation to skull shape; bound feet producing inefficient support and tottering gait; tight-lacing altering chest organs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess observable impairments (gait, respiration, muscular power) and compensatory burdens on other body parts; the essay contrasts apparently normal mental function in some deformed-skull populations with serious functional losses in bound feet or corseted torsos.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medical risk profile / health consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Short- and long-term pathological effects associated with the practice (e.g., headaches, deafness, cerebral congestions, meningitis, cerebritis, epilepsy, idiocy, corns, bunions, ingrowing nails, general weariness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article cites medical observations (especially French physicians on head deformation and surgeons on effects of heels/shoes); use documented clinical sequelae to evaluate harms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pain, distress, and observable suffering during procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the process is painful or produces observable distress (e.g., reports of infants under pressure showing dullness/torpor or not crying; foot-binding described as extremely painful).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider both immediate behavioral indicators (crying, moaning, torpor) and later-life reports; absence of visible crying does not imply absence of harm (author notes torpor or insensibility may mask pain).

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of social enforcement and reputational consequence
rubrics_metrics.description: How strongly the custom is socially enforced and the reputational penalties for noncompliance (e.g., failure to mold a child's cranium gives a mother reputation of being lazy and undutiful).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess social pressure, status associations (chiefs vs slaves), and the role of fashion in maintaining customs even when harmful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevalence, universality and antiquity
rubrics_metrics.description: How widespread, ancient, or culturally independent a practice is (e.g., cranial deformation found worldwide and ancient; certain practices nearly universal in regions like ancient Peru or among Malays).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use archaeological and historical evidence (tombs, classical authors) to gauge cultural persistence and independent origin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recoverability / permanence over life
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the altered form tends to persist permanently or partly regains natural shape during growth (e.g., skulls often permanently altered though may partly regain shape; some pressure applied by hands soon recovers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider developmental plasticity: short, light pressures may be temporary whereas prolonged bandaging or binding produces lasting change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cognitive / behavioral outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Observed effects (if any) upon mental power, intelligence, or social abilities (e.g., general lack of marked difference in mental power between deformed-head groups and neighboring tribes; chiefs with deformed heads rising to eminence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use comparative observation to judge cognitive impact but beware of confounds (nutrition, lifestyle, social organization).

rubrics_metrics.name: Heritability / biological transmission of induced deformity
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether artificially produced deformities can be transmitted by inheritance to offspring (Hippocrates and later writers debate possible occasional transmission but much evidence against habitual inheritance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between cultural transmission (practice passed by custom) and genetic inheritance; the essay suggests occasional reports but not habitual genetic transmission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fit between tools/clothing and natural anatomy (design criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether manufactured items (shoes, boots, heels) are constructed to follow the natural form of the foot (great toe parallel to axis) or impose a symmetric/injurious shape (bilaterally symmetric lasts, pointed toes, high narrow heels).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author recommends designing footwear on the model of the natural foot (avoid bilateral symmetry, accommodate great toe); evaluates current fashion lasts as causing deformity and impaired function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative aesthetic standard: nature vs convention
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether beauty is judged by reference to natural form (nature as standard) or by a purely conventional/fashionable criterion (e.g., admiring constricted waist or pointed foot).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay argues that adopting purely conventional criteria places one on a level with cultures we readily condemn; suggests reflection whether taste is sound and warns of arbitrariness of fashion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification reliability and continuum of variation
rubrics_metrics.description: Difficulty of rigidly classifying deformations because many pass insensibly into one another and vary with perseverance and skill of application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize classifications as heuristic rather than absolute; detailed morphological and methodological description is preferable to rigid categories when forms grade into one another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative social-function criterion (status maintenance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the practice serves to mark social divisions or maintain status (e.g., chiefs' families always deformed while slaves are not permitted; social position maintained irrespective of apparent impairment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether modifications are instruments of social differentiation and thus resilient despite possible harms.
